opus-5.5.text:
The core idea was pretty simple: I wanted to lower the barrier to writing high-performance simulation code. During my PhD, especially working on physically based simulation like the Material Point Method, I kept noticing that a huge fraction of my time wasn't spent on the physics or the numerical method itself. It went into engineering: writing CUDA kernels, managing memory layouts, dealing with sparse data structures, and porting things between CPU and GPU. Every new project, you'd reinvent a lot of the same wheels.

So with Taichi, I hoped to build a layer of infrastructure where researchers, engineers, and even artists and students could write simulation code that looks almost like plain Python, close to how you'd think about the algorithm on paper, and still get performance comparable to hand-tuned GPU code. The compiler should take care of parallelization, data layout, and sparsity, so the person can focus on the creative part.

Beyond performance, I wanted productivity and portability. You write your program once, and it runs on CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, or a CPU backend. That matters a lot if you want simulation to leave the lab and show up in games, film, robotics, or even on phones.

Ultimately, the bigger dream was to make simulation as accessible as, say, deep learning became after frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch. Those tools let many more people experiment with neural networks. I hoped Taichi could do something similar for the physical world: if more people can easily build and play with simulations, we'll get more interesting research, better tools for content creation, and maybe some applications nobody has thought of yet.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I started Taichi, the problem I kept running into as a graphics researcher was that writing a physical simulation meant spending most of my time on things that had nothing to do with the physics. You'd have an idea for a new material model or a new solver, and then you'd spend weeks writing CUDA kernels, managing sparse data structures by hand, worrying about memory layouts, and debugging segfaults. The actual algorithm might be fifty lines of math, and the implementation would be thousands of lines of low-level code that only ran on one kind of hardware.

So the goal with Taichi was really to separate what you want to compute from how it gets computed. I wanted someone to be able to write a simulation that looks almost like the pseudocode in the paper, in Python, and have it compile down to something that runs fast on GPUs or CPUs without the author being a performance engineer. If you can do that, you change who gets to do simulation. Grad students, indie game developers, people in robotics or computational fabrication, they can all iterate quickly instead of fighting the machine.

The infrastructure framing matters to me because simulation is becoming a substrate for a lot of other things. It's not just making pretty animations anymore. It's generating training data, it's differentiable physics for learning controllers, it's digital twins, it's prototyping hardware before you build it. If the compute layer is easy to express and portable across hardware, then all of those downstream applications get cheaper. That was the bet: make the low-level pain go away, and let people spend their time on the ideas.

Researchers often have an idea they want to explore, but then spend a huge amount of time dealing with low-level implementation and optimization. The goal was to let them express the computation in a concise, intuitive way, while the compiler handles much of the work of running it efficiently on parallel hardware. Hopefully, that means people can spend more time experimenting with new ideas and less time wrestling with the infrastructure.
